claim: COVID-19 is a systemic disease based on clinical observations.
source: Clinical observations indicate that COVID-19 is a systemic disease.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by clinical observations referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study analyzed 61 tissues and organs from 11 deceased COVID-19 patients.
source: We present a detailed mapping of the viral RNA in 61 tissues and organs of 11 deceased patients with COVID-19.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and describes the study design.

claim: Autopsies were performed within an early postmortem interval of 1.5 to 15 hours with a mean of 5.6 hours.
source: The autopsies were performed within the early postmortem interval (between 1.5 and 15 hr, mean: 5.6 hr) to minimize the bias due to viral RNA and tissue degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and describes the methodology to minimize degradation bias.

claim: Very high viral loads (>10^4 copies/ml) were detected in most patients' lungs.
source: Very high viral loads (>104copies/ml) were detected in most patients' lungs, and the presence of intact viral particles in the lung tissue could be verified by transmission electron microscopy.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in the results and figures.

claim: Intact viral particles were verified in lung tissue by transmission electron microscopy.
source: Very high viral loads (>104copies/ml) were detected in most patients' lungs, and the presence of intact viral particles in the lung tissue could be verified by transmission electron microscopy.
evidence: This is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 2.

claim: Viral RNA was detected throughout various extrapulmonary tissues and organs without visible tissue damage.
source: Interestingly, viral RNA was detected throughout various extrapulmonary tissues and organs without visible tissue damage.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load mapping data in Figure 1 and histopathological analysis.

claim: The dissemination of SARS-CoV-2 RNA throughout the body supports the hypothesis of a maladaptive host response with viremia and multiorgan dysfunction.
source: The dissemination of SARS-CoV-2-RNA throughout the body supports the hypothesis that there is a maladaptive host response with viremia and multiorgan dysfunction.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the viral RNA distribution data presented in the study.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 was first described in Wuhan, China in December 2019.
source: In December 2019, several cases of pneumonia caused by a novel Betacoronavirus called SARS-CoV-2 were first described in the city of Wuhan in China (Zhu et al., 2020); the disease was thereafter named 'coronavirus disease 2019' (COVID-19) (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: More than 121 million SARS-CoV-2 infections have been reported worldwide.
source: At present, more than 121 million SARS-CoV-2 infections have been reported (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to epidemiological data.

claim: The number of deaths attributed to COVID-19 has exceeded 2.6 million worldwide.
source: The number of deaths attributed to COVID-19 has exceeded 2.6 million worldwide (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to epidemiological data.

claim: Approximately 81% of COVID-19 patients experience mild symptoms.
source: While approximately 81% of COVID-19 patients experience mild symptoms, 14% suffer from respiratory distress, and 5% have to be hospitalized (Wu and McGoogan, 2020; Wiersinga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: 14% of COVID-19 patients suffer from respiratory distress.
source: While approximately 81% of COVID-19 patients experience mild symptoms, 14% suffer from respiratory distress, and 5% have to be hospitalized (Wu and McGoogan, 2020; Wiersinga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: 5% of COVID-19 patients have to be hospitalized.
source: While approximately 81% of COVID-19 patients experience mild symptoms, 14% suffer from respiratory distress, and 5% have to be hospitalized (Wu and McGoogan, 2020; Wiersinga et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: 20% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients enter a critical condition with respiratory failure, endovascular complications, or multiple organ dysfunction.
source: Of these, 20% enter a critical condition with respiratory failure, endovascular complications, or multiple organ dysfunction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on clinical observations.

claim: Gastroenterological symptoms have been reported in 36.4% of COVID-19 patients.
source: Gastroenterological and neurological symptoms have been reported in 36.4% and 18.6% of COVID-19 patients, respectively, in case studies (Wiersinga et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to case studies.

claim: Neurological symptoms have been reported in 18.6% of COVID-19 patients.
source: Gastroenterological and neurological symptoms have been reported in 36.4% and 18.6% of COVID-19 patients, respectively, in case studies (Wiersinga et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to case studies.

claim: ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are crucial for SARS-CoV-2 entry into cells.
source: While little information has been available to date about the molecular regulation of SARS-CoV-2 infections, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) and transmembrane protease serine 2 (TMPRSS2), two membrane-bound proteins, have been shown to be crucial for the entry of the virus into cells (Wang et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: ACE2 is expressed in epithelia of the lung and several other epithelial, endothelial, heart, and renal tissues.
source: ACE2 is expressed not only in the epithelia of the lung but also in several other epithelial, endothelial, heart, and renal tissues (Hamming et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on ACE2 expression.

claim: Patients 1-7 received intensive care.
source: In detail, patients 1–7 received intensive care; patients 1–6 were mechanically ventilated, whereas patient 7 was subjected to ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing patient characteristics.

claim: Patients 1-6 were mechanically ventilated.
source: In detail, patients 1–7 received intensive care; patients 1–6 were mechanically ventilated, whereas patient 7 was subjected to ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing patient characteristics.

claim: Patient 7 was subjected to ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).
source: In detail, patients 1–7 received intensive care; patients 1–6 were mechanically ventilated, whereas patient 7 was subjected to ECMO (extracorporeal membrane oxygenation).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing patient characteristics.

claim: Patients 1-2 and 5-6 were treated with lopinavir/ritonavir.
source: Patients 1–2 and 5–6 were treated with lopinavir/ritonavir.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing patient treatment.

claim: Patients 8-10 were not subjected to intensive care or ventilation according to their patient provisions.
source: Patients 8–10 were not subjected to intensive care or ventilation according to their patient provisions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing patient characteristics.

claim: Patients 1-10 died of COVID-19.
source: Our results show that patients 1–10 died of COVID-19, whereas patient 11 suffered from a metastasized squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and died of an ileus following peritoneal carcinosis (Table 2 provides an overview of the macro- and micromorphological autopsy findings).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on autopsy findings.

claim: Patient 11 suffered from a metastasized squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and died of an ileus following peritoneal carcinosis.
source: Our results show that patients 1–10 died of COVID-19, whereas patient 11 suffered from a metastasized squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and died of an ileus following peritoneal carcinosis (Table 2 provides an overview of the macro- and micromorphological autopsy findings).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on autopsy findings.

claim: Patient 11 had contracted COVID-19 and received intensive care treatment but was not ventilated.
source: Patient 11 had contracted COVID-19 and received intensive care treatment but was not ventilated.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing patient 11's clinical course.

claim: Autopsy detected previously undiagnosed chronic lymphatic leukemia (CLL) in patient 2.
source: Interestingly, autopsy detected previously undiagnosed malignancies in patients 2 (chronic lymphatic leukemia, CLL) and 10 (endometrial carcinoma).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on autopsy findings.

claim: Autopsy detected previously undiagnosed endometrial carcinoma in patient 10.
source: Interestingly, autopsy detected previously undiagnosed malignancies in patients 2 (chronic lymphatic leukemia, CLL) and 10 (endometrial carcinoma).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on autopsy findings.

claim: Patient 6 had an incidentaloma of the thyroid gland.
source: In addition, patient 6 had an incidentaloma of the thyroid gland.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on autopsy findings.

claim: High to moderate to low viral loads were detected in other structures of the respiratory tract, such as the mesopharynx, epiglottis and trachea, in patients 1-8.
source: High to moderate to low viral loads were detected in other structures of the respiratory tract, such as the mesopharynx, epiglottis and trachea, in patients 1–8.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In patient 11, vRNA could only be detected in moderate to low amounts in the trachea.
source: In patient 11, with a non-COVID-19-associated cause of death, vRNA could only be detected in moderate to low amounts in the trachea.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Patients 1-10 showed variable viral loads in at least two samples obtained from the lymphatic system.
source: Patients 1–10 also showed variable (very high to very low) viral loads in at least two samples obtained from the lymphatic system.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Lymphatic structures with topological relationships to the respiratory tract were always positive for vRNA.
source: Lymphatic structures with topological relationships to the respiratory tract were always positive for vRNA.
evidence: This is an observation based on the viral load data.

claim: Patients 1, 3, 4, and 5 exhibited moderate to very low viral loads in cardiac samples.
source: Of the patients subjected to intensive care treatment (patients 1–7), patients 1, 3, 4, and 5 exhibited moderate to very low viral loads in the cardiac samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Patients 2, 6, and 7 exhibited no vRNA in the heart muscle.
source: Patients 2, 6, and 7 exhibited no vRNA in the heart muscle.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Vascular samples exhibited higher viral loads overall than cardiac samples in the majority of patients.
source: The vascular samples exhibited higher viral loads overall than the cardiac samples in the majority of patients.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing viral load data between vascular and cardiac tissues.

claim: Viral RNA was detected in the blood only for patients 3-5.
source: Viral RNA was detected in the blood only for patients 3–5.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Patients 1, 2, 6, and 7, who were treated with lopinavir/ritonavir, were negative for vRNA in blood.
source: Patients 1, 2, 6, and 7, who were treated with lopinavir/ritonavir, were negative for vRNA in blood.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data and treatment information.

claim: Viral RNA was present in the bone marrow of all three patients who tested positive for vRNA in blood.
source: Viral RNA was present in the bone marrow of all three patients who tested positive for vRNA in blood and was also found in an additional three patients who tested negative for vRNA in blood.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Viral RNA was found in the bone marrow of an additional three patients who tested negative for vRNA in blood.
source: Viral RNA was present in the bone marrow of all three patients who tested positive for vRNA in blood and was also found in an additional three patients who tested negative for vRNA in blood.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Patients 3-5 had vRNA in variable amounts throughout the small and large intestine.
source: Patients 3–5 had vRNA in variable amounts throughout the small and large intestine.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Patients 6 and 7 tested negative for all 12 gastrointestinal samples.
source: Patients 6 and 7 tested negative for all 12 gastrointestinal samples.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: In patient 9, almost all the gastrointestinal samples exhibited moderate to very high viral loads.
source: Of note, in patient 9, almost all the gastrointestinal samples exhibited moderate to very high viral loads.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Viral RNA could be detected in endocrine organs, in the urinary tract and in the reproductive organs.
source: Viral RNA could also be detected in endocrine organs, in the urinary tract and in the reproductive organs.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Only patients 3-5 tested positive for vRNA in the central nervous system.
source: Only patients 3–5 tested positive for vRNA in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Skin (abdominal), subcutaneous tissue (abdominal) and skeletal muscle (psoas major) tested negative in all patients.
source: Skin (abdominal), subcutaneous tissue (abdominal) and skeletal muscle (psoas major) tested negative in all patients.
evidence: This is supported by the viral load data.

claim: Intact SARS-CoV-2 viral particles were detected within lung fibrocytes of patient 3 by TEM.
source: Due to the very early postmortem interval in which the autopsies were performed, we were able to verify the vRNA findings via TEM of a lung sample from patient 3 by detecting intact SARS-CoV-2 viral particles within lung fibrocytes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 2.

claim: IL-6 serum levels were significantly elevated in all COVID-19 patients compared to healthy volunteers.
source: Both parameters showed significantly elevated serum levels in all cases compared to the levels in five healthy volunteers, who served as controls.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: IL-8 serum levels were significantly elevated in all COVID-19 patients compared to healthy volunteers.
source: Both parameters showed significantly elevated serum levels in all cases compared to the levels in five healthy volunteers, who served as controls.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPa) serum levels were significantly higher in COVID-19 patients than in healthy volunteers.
source: Our results showed significantly higher serum levels of tissue plasminogen activator (tPa) (Figure 3c) in COVID-19 patients than in healthy volunteers.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: P-Selectin was found in all patients in serum at levels significantly higher than those in controls.
source: P-Selectin (Figure 3d), a cell adhesion molecule in platelets necessary for the recruitment of platelets and binding to the endothelium (Furie and Furie, 2004), was found in all patients in serum at levels significantly higher than those in controls.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3d and a citation to the function of P-Selectin.

claim: D dimer serum levels were slightly elevated in patients but no significant elevation could be found.
source: D dimer serum levels (Figure 3e) were slightly elevated in patients. However, no significant elevation could be found.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI) was significantly elevated in the blood serum of all patients.
source: The level of plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI, Figure 3f), an important inhibitor of tPa (Cesari et al., 2010), was significantly elevated in the blood serum of all patients.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3f and a citation to PAI function.

claim: sCD40L was significantly elevated in all patients.
source: The level of a biomarker with potential for cardiovascular risk stratification, sCD40L (Figure 3g), was significantly elevated in all patients.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Coagulation factor IX was measured at significantly elevated levels in the blood serum of all patients.
source: Furthermore, coagulation factor IX (Figure 3h) was measured at significantly elevated levels in the blood serum of all patients; it has been proposed to function as a mediator between viruses and cells (Lenman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3h and a citation to its proposed function.

claim: The level of P-Selectin Glykoprotein Ligand-1 (PSGL-1) was determined to be not significantly higher in patients than in the healthy volunteer group.
source: The level of P-Selectin Glykoprotein Ligand-1 (PSGL-1) was determined to be not significantly higher in patients than in the healthy volunteer group.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Macroscopic signs of severe and extensive lung damage were found in all patients.
source: Macroscopic signs of severe and extensive lung damage were found in all patients.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing macroscopic findings.

claim: In patients 1, 3-5, 9, and 10, the lung tissue was full of blood (hyperemia) and fluid (edema) and showed weakened consistency.
source: In patients 1, 3–5, 9, and 10, the lung tissue was full of blood (hyperemia) and fluid (edema) and showed weakened consistency (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is supported by macroscopic observations and images in Figure 4a,b.

claim: The lungs of patients 6-8 displayed a firmer and more consolidated pattern with only a low degree of edema and hyperemia.
source: In contrast, the lungs of patients 6–8 displayed a firmer and more consolidated pattern with only a low degree of edema and hyperemia (Figure 4c–e).
evidence: This is supported by macroscopic observations and images in Figure 4c-e.

claim: In the lungs of patient 3, nodular demarcated damage was found that was correlated with fungal superinfection.
source: In the lungs of patient 3, nodular demarcated damage was found that was correlated with fungal superinfection (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by macroscopic observations and images in Figure 4f.

claim: Patients 6, 9, and 10 had purulent bronchitis and bronchopneumonia due to bacterial superinfection.
source: Patients 6, 9, and 10 had purulent bronchitis and bronchopneumonia due to bacterial superinfection, and patient nine exhibited severe pharyngitis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing macroscopic findings.

claim: Patient 9 exhibited severe pharyngitis.
source: Patients 6, 9, and 10 had purulent bronchitis and bronchopneumonia due to bacterial superinfection, and patient nine exhibited severe pharyngitis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing macroscopic findings.

claim: Several features of coagulopathies were found, including infarction of the lung and the spleen as well as fulminant thromboses of the periprostatic venous plexus and hemorrhage of the cerebellum.
source: Several features of coagulopathies were found, including infarction of the lung (Figure 4g) and the spleen (Figure 4h) as well as fulminant thromboses of the periprostatic venous plexus (Figure 4i) and hemorrhage of the cerebellum (Figure 4j).
evidence: This is supported by macroscopic observations and images in Figure 4g-j.

claim: Vascular stasis and fibrinous thrombi were present in patients 1-2 and 8-10.
source: Vascular stasis and fibrinous thrombi were present in patients 1–2 and 8–10.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing macroscopic findings.

claim: Thrombemboli were found in patients 2, 4, 5, and 10 to a variable extent.
source: Thrombemboli were found in patients 2, 4, 5, and 10 to a variable extent.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing macroscopic findings.

claim: In patient 2, pulmonary embolisms were fatal.
source: In patient 2, pulmonary embolisms were fatal.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing macroscopic findings.

claim: The lung tissues from patients 1, 3-5, 9, and 10 revealed changes consistent with the early (exudative) phase of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD).
source: Microscopically, the lung tissues from patients 1, 3–5, 9, and 10 revealed changes consistent with the early (exudative) phase of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing microscopic findings.

claim: The consistent acute changes in lungs included severe intraalveolar and interstitial hemorrhages, architectural injuries with a diffuse alveolar damage pattern, sporadic signs of cellular inflammation, and severe loss of structured pneumocytes.
source: The consistent acute changes included severe intraalveolar and interstitial hemorrhages (Figure 5a, Figure 5b), architectural injuries with a diffuse alveolar damage pattern (involving hyaline membranes, fibrinous edema and interstitial proliferation), sporadic signs of cellular inflammation (mostly involving lymphocytes and a few plasma cells) and severe loss of structured pneumocytes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Cells with an enlarged cytoplasm and large nuclei were found to be admixed with multinucleated giant cells and to show features of squamous metaplasia and a pattern of bronchiolization.
source: Frequently, cells with an enlarged cytoplasm and large nuclei were found to be admixed with multinucleated giant cells and to show features of squamous metaplasia and a pattern of bronchiolization (Figure 5a,b,c).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 5a,b,c.

claim: Enlarged alveolar cells were detached from the alveolar wall.
source: Enlarged alveolar cells were detached from the alveolar wall (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 5d.

claim: The clusters of enlarged cells were strongly positive for AE1/3.
source: The clusters of enlarged cells were strongly positive for AE1/3 (Figure 5e), but only a few cells were colabeled with TTF1 (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Only a few enlarged cells were colabeled with TTF1.
source: The clusters of enlarged cells were strongly positive for AE1/3 (Figure 5e), but only a few cells were colabeled with TTF1 (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The lung histology in patients 6-8 displayed a pattern similar to the latter (proliferative) phase of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD).
source: The lung histology in patients 6–8 displayed a pattern similar to the latter (proliferative) phase of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing microscopic findings.

claim: Giant cells and cell aggregates resembling squamous metaplasia were frequently found and sometimes accompanied by fibroblastic proliferation in patients 6-8.
source: Giant cells and cell aggregates resembling squamous metaplasia were frequently found and sometimes accompanied by fibroblastic proliferation (Figure 5g,h).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 5g,h.

claim: The upper lobes of the lung of patient 2 showed only moderate emphysema.
source: While the upper lobes of the lung of patient 2 showed only moderate emphysema (Figure 6a), the hemorrhagic tissue damage was restricted to the middle and lower lobes of the right and the lower lobe of the left lung (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 6a.

claim: The hemorrhagic tissue damage in patient 2 was restricted to the middle and lower lobes of the right and the lower lobe of the left lung.
source: While the upper lobes of the lung of patient 2 showed only moderate emphysema (Figure 6a), the hemorrhagic tissue damage was restricted to the middle and lower lobes of the right and the lower lobe of the left lung (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 6b.

claim: Vasculitis-like features were observed in patients 2, 3, 4, 8, and 9 with sporadic mild lymphoplasmatic cellular infiltrates around the pulmonary artery branches.
source: Vasculitis-like features were observed in patients 2, 3, 4, 8, and 9 with sporadic mild lymphoplasmatic cellular infiltrates around the pulmonary artery branches (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 6c,d.

claim: In patient 7, a strong lymphocyte-predominant intra-alveolar infiltrate was found.
source: However, in patient 7, a strong lymphocyte-predominant intra-alveolar infiltrate was found (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 6e,f.

claim: Megakaryocytes were sometimes detectable in alveolar capillaries.
source: In particular, megakaryocytes were sometimes detectable in alveolar capillaries (Figure 6g,h).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 6g,h.

claim: A common histological feature in all patients was the loss of the follicular architecture of the lymph nodes due to architectural changes.
source: A common histological feature in all patients was the loss of the follicular architecture of the lymph nodes due to architectural changes (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 7a.

claim: In the bone marrow of patient 9, the highest viral loads were found, and significant hemophagocytosis was detectable by microscopy.
source: In the bone marrow of patient 9, the highest viral loads were found, and significant hemophagocytosis was detectable by microscopy (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by viral load data and microscopic observations shown in Figure 7b.

claim: A correlation between a high viral load and tissue damage, as seen in the lung, was not found in cardiac or aortic tissues.
source: Interestingly, a correlation between a high viral load and tissue damage, as seen in the lung, was not found in cardiac or aortic tissues.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing viral loads with histopathological findings.

claim: The cardiac tissues sometimes showed pre-existing changes (fibrosis and chronic ischemic damage), but no severe damage, inflammation or necrosis of cardiomyocytes was found.
source: The cardiac tissues sometimes showed pre-existing changes (fibrosis and chronic ischemic damage), but no severe damage, inflammation or necrosis of cardiomyocytes was found (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 7c.

claim: An increase in cellularity in the otherwise unremarkable cardiac tissue was seen in patient 1, which was suggestive of an activated cardio-mesenchyme.
source: Sometimes an increase in cellularity in the otherwise unremarkable cardiac tissue was seen (e.g. in patient 1), which was suggestive of an activated cardio-mesenchyme (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 7d.

claim: The large vessels were unremarkable.
source: The large vessels were unremarkable as well.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing microscopic findings.

claim: The thoracic aorta of patient 5 showed no inflammatory cells or tissue damage despite testing highly positive for vRNA.
source: Figure 6e demonstrates a section of the thoracic aorta of patient 5 obtained from the same anatomical location as the sample that tested highly positive for vRNA. Neither the intima (asterisk) nor the upper tunica media displayed any inflammatory cells or tissue damage.
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 7e,f (note: text refers to Figure 6e but likely means Figure 7e based on context).

claim: In the colonic mucosa, strong signs of epithelial damage were not visible by light microscopy.
source: In the colonic mucosa, strong signs of epithelial damage were not visible by light microscopy (e.g. patient 3; Figure 7g), and the histology of the pancreas was well preserved (e.g. patient 9; Figure 7h).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 7g.

claim: The histology of the pancreas was well preserved.
source: In the colonic mucosa, strong signs of epithelial damage were not visible by light microscopy (e.g. patient 3; Figure 7g), and the histology of the pancreas was well preserved (e.g. patient 9; Figure 7h).
evidence: This is supported by microscopic observations and images in Figure 7h.

claim: Many critically ill COVID-19 patients show multiple organ involvement in addition to lung failure, in particular vascular dysfunction, including thrombosis and/or impaired microcirculation.
source: In clinical practice, many critically ill COVID-19 patients show multiple organ involvement in addition to lung failure, in particular vascular dysfunction, including thrombosis and/or impaired microcirculation (Ji et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to clinical observations.

claim: A dysregulated immune response was observed in COVID-19, starting with a phase of immunosuppression followed by a proinflammatory phase and then a cytokine storm.
source: A dysregulated immune response was observed, starting with a phase of immunosuppression followed by a proinflammatory phase and then a cytokine storm (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to immunological studies.

claim: The cytokine storm may play an important role in COVID-19, which supports the hypothesis that COVID-19 could have a strong immunopathological component.
source: The cytokine storm may play an important role in COVID-19, which supports the hypothesis that COVID-19 could have a strong immunopathological component.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed cytokine storm phenomenon.

claim: SARS-CoV can infect nasal mucous cells, pneumocytes and alveolar macrophages.
source: Some aspects of the viral pathogenesis and the toxicity of the novel virus SARS-CoV-2 are known based on previous studies of SARS-CoV (Qian et al., 2013). The virus can infect nasal mucous cells, pneumocytes and alveolar macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to studies on SARS-CoV.

claim: ACE2 is the main receptor for the cellular binding process of SARS-CoV-2.
source: ACE2 is the main receptor for the cellular binding process (Bar-On et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to molecular studies.

claim: The present study is the only one to date that has measured viral loads in a wide variety of organs and tissues by obtaining and processing 61 samples per patient.
source: However, we analyzed a considerably larger number of organs and tissues than the other groups. To our knowledge, the present study is the only one to date that has measured viral loads in a wide variety of organs and tissues by obtaining and processing 61 samples per patient.
evidence: This is a claim about the uniqueness of the study design compared to other published studies.

claim: The present study is the only study so far that has focused on keeping the postmortem interval as short as possible to avoid bias due to the degradation of SARS-CoV-2 virus particles, SARS-CoV-2 RNA and tissue ultrastructure.
source: The present study is the only study so far that has focused on keeping the postmortem interval as short as possible to avoid bias due to the degradation of SARS-CoV-2 virus particles, SARS-CoV-2 RNA and tissue ultrastructure.
evidence: This is a claim about the uniqueness of the study design compared to other published studies.

claim: The duration of post-mortem intervals in this study did not substantially influence the vRNA copy numbers.
source: From Table 2 it becomes clear that the duration of post-mortem intervals in our study did not substantially influence the vRNA copy numbers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in Table 2.

claim: The importance of obtaining multiple samples from within one organ is emphasized by the results of patient 10, in which only two of seven samples from the heart were positive.
source: The importance of obtaining multiple samples from within one organ is emphasized by the results of patient 10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in which only two of seven samples from the heart were positive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the viral load data from patient 10.

claim: If only one sample had been obtained from patient 10's heart, the result of viral detection could have been a false negative.
source: If only one sample had been obtained, the result of viral detection could have been a false negative.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation from patient 10.

claim: The morphologically intact virus particles were located in lung fibrocytes.
source: The morphologically intact virus particles were located in lung fibrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: In lung tissues, the morphology of the viral particles was clearly observed, whereas in other tissues such as liver, heart, and intestine, viral inclusions were not visible by TEM.
source: In lung tissues, the morphology of the viral particles was clearly observed (Figure 2), whereas in other tissues such as liver, heart, and intestine, viral inclusions were not visible by TEM.
evidence: This is an observation based on TEM analysis of different tissues.

claim: The loss of structural hallmarks in non-lung tissues could be due to postmortem cell and tissue turnover and the reduced integrity of virus particles during TEM-related preparations.
source: The loss of structural hallmarks could be due to postmortem cell and tissue turnover and the reduced integrity of virus particles during TEM-related preparations.
evidence: This is a speculation about why viral particles were not visible in some tissues.

claim: The molecular detection of the virus does not depend on the presence of morphologically intact virus particles.
source: It has to be stressed that the molecular detection of the virus does not depend on the presence of morphologically intact virus particles.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of molecular detection methods.

claim: The highest viral loads and the most severe tissue damage were detected in the lungs.
source: We detected the highest viral loads and the most severe tissue damage in the lungs.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from viral load and histopathological data.

claim: The lung samples of all patients showed large cells, sometimes multinucleated giant cells, that were similar to the giant cells described in cases of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection.
